utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'll start with a matter which is of some urgency. Yesterday, transcript page 19809, the Prosecution requested an extension of an additional two weeks to seek leave to reply to the Defence response to the Prosecution's municipalities bar table motion. Could the Defence tell us what their position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Considering that the Defence has no objection, the Chamber will grant the request for an additional two weeks for which the Prosecution now has sought leave, which is granted as well. Considering that the response was distributed on the 19th of November, hereby the Chamber sets the new deadline at the 10th of December. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on the matter. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I deal with the following. On the 22nd of November - last Friday - the Prosecution tendered the document bearing 65 ter number 07153, which subsequently received Exhibit Number P2899. The Chamber notes that the record is unclear about whether the document has been admitted into evidence. This can be found at transcript page numbers 19796 to 97. The Chamber hereby clarifies that P2899 has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Ms. Hasan will now re-examine you. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 25952.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you recall during the cross-examination by Mr. Stojanovic he showed you an aerial image - and that was marked P2922 - of the Batkovic camp. And you identified for us the building where -- that was being prepared for the reception of the prisoners. Now, this is a similar aerial image but one which you marked during your interview in Belgrade in 2010. Is it -- could you identify in this image or tell us which number -- which facility marked by which number is the facility that you made reference to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the facility number 5 --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in this image. Yesterday there was a kind of 1 over it in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer this image into evidence simply because I had previously asked the witness to confirm what he said in his interview which was that he visited facility number 5, and so it's this image that identifies that facility which is the same one marked number 1 on the other image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25952 receives number P2942, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We can remove that image.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, now, yesterday, in response to a question by Defence counsel, you mentioned that you had contacted General Tolimir using extension 165. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 05923, please, displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, you can see from the B/C/S version, and here's the English, that this is the telephone book for the Main Staff of the VRS. It's dated August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't yet have a translation of the page I'm going to refer to in the English, but we will providing be that. For the purposes of my question, I think the B/C/S will suffice. If we could turn to page 20, please, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, can you read the very first line on that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Oh. It's disappeared from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no English translation as was -- yes, that's what -- so, therefore, it doesn't make much sense to try and find it in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I just need the page 20 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not the same -- it is, yes. It's the seam page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, the first -- the first -- not the heading but the very first line on that page, could you please read that aloud to us.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Chief," the extension number is 165.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just above "chief," what -- what does it read there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sector for intelligence and security affairs."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence and we will be providing the English translation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that we don't need all the pages --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so therefore should only this one page and the cover page be sought to be admitted. And then, of course, it is -- yes, the cover page says that it's the telephone directory of the Main Staff, which is relevant and important in this context. So, therefore, we need the cover page, I think, and the translation of this page which is page 20 in B/C/S. And even there, do we need it at all? I mean, if the parties agree that this is the phone book of the Main Staff dated August 1995, where, on page -- printed page 23 and B/C/S page in e-court, it says -- it gives the sector and that number 165 is the number of the chief, then I think we would have everything we need. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I don't know whether you need it for any other reason, Ms. Hasan, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No. If there's an agreement on the record that 165 is the extension of the chief of the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As -- as presented in this --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- as provided by the witness, then that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as presented in this phone book dated August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour. I don't think the Prosecution will have any problem with us saying that it is from August 1995. The conversation that the witness referred to, if it took place, according to the Prosecution, took place before that date. So this document is something that you will attribute weight to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness said for his conversation, 165. And we see in a phone book of August that 165 stands for the chief. Now, if it is the Defence's position that in July that was a different number, then we'll hear from you. This is what we have and this is what we agree upon. I mean, that the phone book says, in August, 165 is the chief, and that the witness has told us that in his recollection that number 165 was used. That's it. And if there's any other interpretation, then it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't want to interpret anything, Your Honours, only in line 15, page 5, Ms. Hasan said that if there is agreement on the record that 165 is the extension of the chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was the chief of this sector and that seems to be the sector on which, in July, as far as I understand the evidence, Mr. Tolimir was the chief, and that 165 therefore would, in the opinion of the Prosecution and perhaps of the Defence as well, be the phone number of the chief of this specific sector. There we are. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn to 65 ter 23538.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Witness, you recall yesterday being cross-examined, and you were asked about the -- the appropriateness of the order that came down from General Tolimir to you vis-à-vis -- in terms of the -- the chain of command. I'd like to show you this document. And what we have here is a document from the -- we see on the top, VRS Main Staff. It's from the intelligence and security administration, and we see here it's dated 29 May 1993. And just below that we see it concerns prisoner exchange commissions work. Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And do you see that this -- this report is addressed to the intelligence departments of various corps, including the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we turn to the second page in the English, and that's also the second page in the B/C/S, we see here that it's from Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, I can give you an opportunity to briefly review the document, if you wish, but I'd like to specifically turn your attention to the very last paragraph. And it says: "In the future, all reports on the work of the commission, POW exchanges, lists of exchanged persons and persons offered for exchange shall be sent by telegram to the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, at the time of this -- this report dated 29th May 1993, were you the chief of the intelligence and security organ in the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. It was as of mid-November 1993 that I assumed that duty. To be more precise, it took place on the 16th of November.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And -- and at the time of this -- of 29 May, do you recall what position you held?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, my duty was in the security administration of the Ministry of the Armed Forces of the FRY, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, this instruction here by then-Colonel Tolimir that all reports on the work of the commission, POW exchanges, lists of exchanged persons and so on and so forth, did that instruction continue to apply at the time you were the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did continue to apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 23538 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23538 receives number P2943, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. No objections were raised. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we now turn to P2143, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, this is a document, and it -- as soon as it shows up on the screen, you'll see it also comes from the Main Staff of the VRS. And it's dated 20 January 1995, so when you did, in fact, hold the position of chief of the security and intelligence organ. Okay. It's up on our screens. Again this -- what is called here an authorisation relates to prisoner exchange and you see here that it is directed to the OBP, abbreviation for the intelligence and security sections, of the Drina Corps and the East Bosnia Corps. And I can give you -- I don't know if you're familiar with this particular document. It deals with the prisoners -- the Lisaca - excuse my pronunciation - prisoners and there are some instructions to the IBK commission in terms of how to deal with them. Are you familiar with this document? Perhaps we can also turn to the very last page where we can see that this is authored by General Tolimir. And it's page 3 of the -- yeah, that's right. Do you see that there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if turn to -- go back to page 2 in the English, and this is page 1, I believe, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And General Tolimir is giving various instructions to the IBK and he also does so to the Drina Corps. And in the second-to-last paragraph, full paragraph, we see: "During the negotiations do not show any interest in the Lisaca prisoners. On the contrary, at an opportune moment misinform them that Lisaca fighters are not an exchange priority because they had surrendered to the enemy side, and that priority will be given to prisoners [sic] involved in offensive combat operations." And General Tolimir goes on to explain that this is essentially a strategy of misinformation in order to get a more favourable exchange. Witness, are you familiar with this instruction that General Tolimir gave on the strategy involving a negotiation for the exchange of these Lisaca prisoners in January 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the document, that is to say, instructions I received, as well as the chief of the intelligence and security organ of the Drina Corps. I read through the -- read the document, and I don't think there's any need for me to comment on its contents. As for the two people from the Drina Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The -- the question simply was whether you are familiar with the document. And I think the simple answer is yes, you are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: This document is already in evidence, so I'll move to the next one, which is 65 ter 19571, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, here, Colonel, we see another document from the Main Staff of the VRS intelligence and security sector. This one is dated a little bit later. We're looking at the 3rd of September, 1995. And, again, the subject matter is the exchange of prisoners, and there's a report here. It is addressed to the commanders and the intelligence and security departments of various corps, including the IBK, the East Bosnia Corps. Do you see that there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 5 in the English, as well as the last page of the B/C/S, which is page 2, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We see that this report is generated by General Tolimir. Again, in September of 1995, General Tolimir is still dealing with the issue of the Lisaca members of the -- VRS members who were captured at Lisaca, as well as Vijenac - and I'm sure I've mispronounced that - and he is reporting and giving instructions on the exchange that is to -- is to take place with captured Muslims held at Batkovic camp. And, of course, this is the camp we've been discussing over the last day. Are you familiar with this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the other -- the page with this information on this document, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Certainly. I can turn your attention perhaps to page 4 of the English, and this would be at page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Where General Tolimir, after essentially addressing the complaints of the East Bosnia Corps and others for the lack of prisoners to exchange to get their -- their soldiers back, he provides the following: "The exchange commission chairmen must view the exchange proposal integrally, as does the Main Staff VRS, since so far the Main Staff has made the necessary number of prisoners available for the corps commissions in circumstances where they did not have a sufficient number of captured enemy soldiers to exchange for all the captured members of the [sic] corps." And he goes on: "Security organs and exchange commission chairmen must also avoid using parents' bitterness because it is not possible to exchange prisoners who have been in prison for quite some time, particularly because the Main Staff VRS is not responsible for this situation, rather, it is the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our units." Witness, I don't know if that refreshes your recollection about this document, but do you -- are you familiar with this and the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document. I wasn't able to read it whole -- to read all of it; but, yes, I know it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd offer 65 ter 19571 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19571 receives number P2944, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Colonel, now we've seen a number of documents here where General Tolimir is reporting on providing instructions, discussing strategy, and to your security and intelligence organ, among others, in relation to exchange of prisoners. Now, is General Tolimir's involvement in these prisoner -- in this prisoner exchange process in line with his duties and his responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, yes; but on the other hand, partly no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You say partly yes and partly no. Is it -- or is he acting outside the line, outside the sphere of his responsibilities in dealing with prisoners' exchange? I mean, you received these instructions. You received these reports. Is that how you took them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpreted this as an instruction giving directions as to what should be done and how. I did not understand this to be an order. If it was meant to be an order, then it is beyond his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Colonel Todorovic, these instructions that tell -- General Tolimir provided, did you at any instance contravene his instructions? Or directions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason not to act pursuant to the documents showed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No one asked you whether there were reasons. The simple question was whether you ever did contravene those instructions. The answer, apparently, is no, if I understood your answer well. Could you please focus on the question and start with a direct answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, in looking at these documents, is there anything that you have seen - and you're familiar with these issues - where General Tolimir was acting outside of his responsibilities and duties in dealing with these matters?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to tell now. But on the whole, no, I can't see anything that is contrary to the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have one final question for you, Colonel, and it's in relation to that paragraph I read to you from the 3rd September 1995 report from General Tolimir, and he -- where he is mentioning -- or he is explaining why there aren't sufficient prisoners to exchange. How do you reconcile General Tolimir's statement about the small number of enemy captured soldiers by the units with his instruction to you just a few months earlier that he was sending 1.000 to 1.200 prisoners to your camp?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reconciliation on my part --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak up. The interpreter didn't understand what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come a bit closer to the microphone and to speak a bit louder so that the interpreters can hear you. And could you please repeat your answer. You started with: "There is no reconciliation on my part," and then you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If all the announced 1.000 to 1200 prisoners had arrived at Batkovic, then there would have been no controversy as to the number of prisoners to be exchanged. Or maybe I should rephrase this and say there would be prisoners for -- for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only a few, Your Honours, with your leave. Could we please get document 13321 from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I would like to skim through this document. It is from the Command of the quarter which you belong, and the date is - and I would like to point this out - the 31st of August, 1995, which is two -- or, rather, three days prior to the document which was shown to you a minute ago and which was authored by General Tolimir. This is addressed to the Main Staff and says, inter alia, and it's General Novica Simic who says so, that on the previous day, on 30 August, a group of 300 parents and members of the families of captured soldiers from Lisaca gathered in the hall of the Ugljevik municipal assembly protesting to your decision to suspend the agreed exchange. The meeting was attended by the president of Ugljevik municipality and some officers from the 1st Majevica Brigade. The commander of the IB corps was also invited to the meeting, but due to the complexity of the situation caused by the bombing, he didn't attend. The atmosphere during the meeting was very tense with the officers being insulted and the same applies to the IBK command and the commander of the VRS. The earlier formed board of parents managed to draw the meeting to a close with the promise that they would request that you urgently see them. An eight-member delegation of the board came to the IBK command at 2000 hours and informed the IBK commander of the meeting and asked me to inform you. And it goes on to say that there were four conclusions or, rather, facts that require an answer. Now that you've seen this document, please tell me if the letter that you have just seen, the instruction or maybe document signed by General Tolimir, could that be the -- the answer to the open issues mentioned here in this document which was sent by Novica Simic to the Main Staff three days earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind -- I apologise. I had to wait for the interpretation. Bearing in mind the extremely difficult situation with the captured Serbian soldiers from Lisaca, from Vijenac, the pressure of the parents which made it so felt daily and the bitterness of their families, would it be exaggerated to say that it was the Main Staff that had a reason and a need to have prisoners of war at that time that they could exchange for members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now finish with one question, and I apologise in advance, Your Honours. I may not be able to give the exact page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But reading your -- the answer you provided on 2 February 1992 [as interpreted], that tells that you were not sure with regard to the telephone extension of General Tolimir and the conversation you had with him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I mentioned number 300-something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was 317.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At some point the investigator mentioned some other numbers to you, 168 and 165, and you said: Yes, these are the numbers, to the best of my memory, of the organ that was above me professionally.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the conclusion be correct that, at that time, you were unable to exactly remember the telephone extension that you used to communicate with at those days?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers stated jogged my memory, and then I accepted that those were the two numbers I dialled frequently but forgot, due to the lapse of time. I was remembered -- I was reminded, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, only for the sake of the record, let us correct page 16, line 14, the statement is of the 2nd of February, 2010, and not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I may have a question which is seeking some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about a -- the exchange of non-Serb population who left Bijeljina, which exchange was organised by Mr. Djurkovic as the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the East Bosnia Corps. And then the question was whether this person had to do anything with the Army of Republika Srpska, and you said he had nothing to do whatsoever with the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska but that, through certain officers, he tried to establish some kind of contact or whatnot, but it was your corps commander, and it was your position as well, "to keep him as far as possible from our task and obligations." Now, the question suggested that Mr. Djurkovic either was or presented himself as the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the East Bosnia Corps. Now, what was it? Was he not the assistant commander? Did he claim to be the assistant commander? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vojkan Djurkovic never had a position in the Army of the RS, and he most certainly was not assistant commander for intelligence and security in the Command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. I don't know if he may have misrepresented himself somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, was his position? Because apparently he was involved in an exchange of non-Serbs. Do you know what his position was, if he was not the assistant, as mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, apart from military exchange commissions, commissions for the exchange of prisoners of war, members of the armed forces, there were also civilian commissions for the exchange of prisoners and population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Such as the state commission, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that may be true, but was there any co-operation between these civilian commissions or -- including the state commission, with the commissions within the structure of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was co-operation but at the highest level; that is, at the level of the Main Staff and the civilian authorities of the RS. Those of us who were lower down received instructions, such as that one that was shown not long ago, instructions as to how to behave in a given situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they not allowed to communicate with the -- with the corps-level commissions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably did communicate, that is, forged provisional agreements, but they needed approval from the exchange commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To communicate or to reach final conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication wasn't prohibited to anyone, but this decision-making was part of the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Instead of "forged" in line 1, it should be "made."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, because I tried to understand what you said about Mr. Djurkovic. You said: He was not within our structures. We should keep away from him as good as we could. But, at the same time, you tell us that he may have been in any civilian commission but that communication with civilian commissions was allowed. So, therefore, I do not -- still do not fully understand what was so special that Mr. Djurkovic had to be kept away from army structures.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This might take some more time, but we don't have enough time. And it isn't necessary either. There was the system of civilian authorities and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second -- one second. Whether we have time and whether we need it is, rather, for me to decide than to be determined by you. Take your time. Explain to us what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of the East Bosnia Corps, especially the town of Bijeljina where the corps command was, the civilian authorities functioned normally, including the civilian police and the structure of state security. That applies also to the army and the Command of the East Bosnia Corps within their limits. Everybody tried to keep their backyards in order without anybody else interfering. For various reasons, that was sometimes justified and other times were not. Vojkan Djurkovic, as far as I knew, but I never -- it was never necessary for me to know him really well. He was engaged in what was called the voluntary exchange of civilians from Bijeljina and the surrounding places against persons from, say, Tuzla. Whether parity was involved in that activity or not, I never made an effort to find out. He never had anything to do with the army expect for the fact that sometimes he requested free passage through the front line, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, again, I still do not understand, when there are civilian authorities dealing with exchange, why this person was to be kept away and not to be talked about; whereas communication with civilian exchange authorities was -- was normal and ...

utterances.speaker: MILENKO TODOROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, if that was something he did on behalf of the authorities, it was someone from the authorities who had to contact the army and tell them that Vojkan was doing that legally and so on. Instead of him popping up on various occasions where he was misplaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Have my questions triggered any need for further questions? If not, Mr. Todorovic, this then concludes your evidence, and I'd like to thank you very much for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you either by the parties or by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is protective measures of closed session so may I suggest we do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we moved into closed session - we would do that, by the way, after the break - I would like to inform the parties that for the next two weeks - so that's starting next week - we'll sit the usual morning-hour sessions, and I think we have exempted the 4th and 11th of December, being Wednesdays, we'll sit in Courtroom II. And I wonder whether now the matter has been resolved, the Defence is willing to withdraw its motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are withdrawing our motion since it is moot now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it has become moot. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00, but we then immediately start in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I dealt with the Chamber's decision in relation to 65 ter number 30493 which had been MFI'd as P2946. The consequence of our decision is that P2946 now is admitted into evidence, under seal. Then we have another four documents which were MFI'd; that is, P2947 up to and including P2950. As a consequence of the earlier decision and having heard further submissions by the parties on these documents, the Chamber admits all four of them into evidence, all under seal. We -- I hoped I would have time to deliver some decisions. We don't have that time. Therefore, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow -- tomorrow, Wednesday, the 27th of November, Courtroom III, 9.30 in the morning. And I already would like to thank, at this moment, everyone who made it possible to conclude the testimony of the last witness today. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of November, 2013, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.25 p.m.,
